carousel.body: Ignore size and importance and work in deadline order. This minimises how late the worst item ends up being.

carousel.title: For value, weigh by density
carousel.body: Divide each job's importance by how long it takes and do the highest ratio first. Long important work loses to quick important work.

carousel.title: Then stop rescheduling
carousel.body: Every reprioritisation is time not spent working. When new items arrive constantly, a fixed rule beats continuous reoptimisation.

sparks.hook: Thinking longer about a decision can make the decision worse.
sparks.insight: A model that fits its training data too closely learns the noise as well as the signal, then performs badly on anything new. People do this too. Elaborate criteria for a hire, a house or a partner are often fitted to a small number of past experiences that were partly luck. Deliberately using less information, with simpler rules and fewer factors and faster decisions, can generalise better, which is why an experienced snap judgement sometimes beats a spreadsheet.
sparks.why: This is one of the book's strongest analogies because the mathematics genuinely transfers: with limited noisy data, a simpler model has lower expected error even though it fits the data you have less well.
sparks.apply: Cut your next decision criteria down to the three factors that matter most, and decide using only those three.

sparks.hook: Offering someone unlimited choice is a cost you are handing them.
sparks.insight: Asking when are you free is generous in intent and expensive in practice, because it makes the other person search their whole calendar and guess at your constraints. Offering three specific times is a smaller gift that costs them almost nothing. The same applies to open-ended briefs, menus with a hundred items, and any request that outsources the hard part of a problem while appearing polite about it.
sparks.why: The cost of a request is the work it creates, not the words it contains. Constraining a problem for someone is usually more helpful than expanding their options.
sparks.apply: Replace your next open invitation with two or three concrete proposals and watch how much faster the thread resolves.

sparks.hook: How long something has already lasted tells you how long it will last.
sparks.insight: For quantities that follow a power-law pattern, such as film revenues or company lifespans, the best guess for the total is a multiple of what has happened so far, so a run that has lasted longer will probably last longer still. For quantities clustered around an average, such as human lifespan, the opposite holds. Getting predictions right requires knowing which kind of distribution you are in, and most everyday errors come from applying the wrong one.
sparks.why: This depends entirely on having a correct prior about the distribution. Applied to the wrong quantity it produces confident nonsense, which is a fair criticism of casual Bayesian reasoning generally.
sparks.apply: Before your next estimate, ask whether the thing clusters around a typical value or has no typical value at all.

sparks.hook: Most things you sort will never be searched enough to justify it.
sparks.insight: Sorting is expensive and only pays off if the collection gets searched often. Computers face this trade constantly and frequently choose not to sort. So do sensible people: an unsorted inbox with good search costs less than a filing system you maintain forever and consult twice a year. The question is not whether order is nicer but whether the number of future searches justifies the ongoing cost of maintaining it.
sparks.why: Sorting cost grows faster than linearly with collection size while search benefit accrues one lookup at a time, so large, rarely-searched collections should usually be left alone.
sparks.apply: Pick one collection you keep organised and count how many times you searched it last month. If it is under five, stop maintaining the order.

sparks.hook: Some bad outcomes are the rules' fault, not the players' fault.
sparks.insight: When everyone acting rationally produces a result nobody wants, whether an arms race, a bidding war, or a culture of late nights because leaving early looks bad, telling people to behave better does not work. The equilibrium is the problem. Changing the rules so the destructive move stops paying, by capping the auction, mandating the holiday, or removing the visible signal, is what actually shifts the behaviour.
sparks.why: This holds where the structure genuinely drives the behaviour. It also gets overused as an excuse in situations where individual choices really were the dominant factor.
sparks.apply: Find one behaviour on your team that everyone dislikes and nobody stops, then change the rule that makes it rational instead of asking people to stop.

sparks.hook: The mathematics is exact. Your life is not the problem it solved.
sparks.insight: Every clean result here assumes something: a known number of options, no recall, independent trials, a stable environment, a well-defined objective. Real decisions rarely supply any of that. The value is not that you can compute your way through a marriage. It is that naming the structure of a problem tells you where the difficulty actually sits, and stops you feeling bad about a decision that was provably impossible to get right.
sparks.why: Critics of the book make exactly this point, that the analogies are looser than the confident framing suggests. The reasonable reply is that an approximate grasp of the structure still beats no structure at all.
sparks.apply: For your next hard decision, write down which assumption of the clean version your situation breaks, and decide with that in view.

actions: Pick one open-ended search you are in the middle of, set an explicit looking period, and commit to deciding at the end of it.
Name what you are minimising this week, whether waiting, lateness or wasted value, and reorder your task list to serve only that.
Count how often you searched your most carefully organised collection last month, and stop maintaining the order if the answer is low.
Take one team behaviour everyone dislikes but nobody stops, and change the rule that makes it the rational choice.
not_for_you_if: You want either rigorous mathematics or direct life advice. It sits in between, and the analogies stretch in places where real life breaks the assumptions.

verification.notes: First published 2016. The optimal stopping and scheduling results are established mathematics; the applications to personal decisions are analogies whose assumptions frequently do not hold.

title: Chip War
subtitle: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology
author: Chris Miller
why_it_matters: It explained why a single company in the Netherlands and a single foundry in Taiwan sit at the centre of world politics. Since it appeared, chip export controls have become one of the main instruments of great-power competition.

crux.headline: Modern power runs through a handful of factories
crux.body: Almost everything, from weapons and cars to phones and machine learning, depends on advanced chips, and advanced chips depend on a supply chain with single points of failure in a few countries. Decades of specialisation produced enormous efficiency and extraordinary fragility at the same time. Whoever controls the machines that make the machines holds leverage that no amount of domestic spending replaces quickly.

sparks.hook: One machine, made by one company, is required for every advanced chip.
sparks.insight: The tool that prints the finest circuit patterns using extreme ultraviolet light is produced by a single Dutch firm, drawing on components from a small number of specialised suppliers. There is no second source anywhere. That single dependency is why restrictions on one product can constrain an entire country's industry, and it is the sharpest example of how decades of efficiency-driven specialisation created chokepoints that nobody designed on purpose.
sparks.why: The concentration is the result of extreme capital costs and physics so demanding that few firms could afford the decades of research. This monopoly was earned rather than engineered.
sparks.apply: Map your own product's supply chain down to individual suppliers and mark every component that has no viable second source.

carousel.title: List the single sources
carousel.body: Walk your bill of materials and mark every component with exactly one supplier. Include software, services and the tools your suppliers themselves depend on.

carousel.title: Time the substitute
carousel.body: Not whether an alternative exists, but how many months of qualification, retooling and testing before it ships. That number is your real exposure.

carousel.title: Look one layer deeper
carousel.body: Your suppliers have single sources too. Most severe shortages arrive from a tier you have never contracted with and cannot see from where you sit.

carousel.title: Price the insurance
carousel.body: Second sources, buffer stock and design flexibility all cost money. Decide deliberately what you will pay rather than discovering it during a shortage.

sparks.hook: The most valuable factories on earth sit beside the tensest strait on earth.
sparks.insight: Leading-edge manufacturing capacity for the world's most advanced chips is concentrated in Taiwan, largely inside one company. That happened for commercial reasons, because a business model that manufactured for everyone and competed with nobody was extremely attractive, not as anyone's strategic choice. The result is that a political crisis in one place would halt production of components every major economy depends on, which is why governments treat the question so seriously.
sparks.why: Analysts disagree sharply over whether this concentration deters conflict by making Taiwan valuable to everyone, or invites it. Both arguments rest on exactly the same fact.
sparks.apply: For your organisation's most critical input, write the one-page answer to what you do if it becomes unavailable for six months.

sparks.hook: Splitting design from manufacturing quietly restructured a whole industry.
sparks.insight: For decades a chip company made its own chips. Then one firm offered to manufacture other people's designs without selling competing products of its own, and the industry split in two. Designers no longer needed a factory, which collapsed the cost of entry and produced a wave of new companies. It also concentrated manufacturing into fewer and fewer hands, because each generation of factory cost more than the last one did.
sparks.why: This is a specialisation story with a predictable ending: falling entry costs on one side, rising capital requirements and consolidation on the other, both flowing from the same decision.
sparks.apply: Find one capability your company owns because it always has, and price what buying it from a specialist would actually cost.

carousel.title: Separate the design
carousel.body: Chip designers stopped needing factories. Entry costs collapsed and a generation of firms appeared that could never have afforded to build anything themselves.

carousel.title: Concentrate the manufacturing
carousel.body: Each new generation of factory cost more than the last, so fewer firms could stay at the leading edge. Efficiency and fragility rose together.

carousel.title: Specialise the tools
carousel.body: Equipment makers, materials suppliers and design software each became a near-monopoly, because each required decades of accumulated practical know-how.

carousel.title: Notice the chokepoints
carousel.body: The chain works beautifully until one link is denied. Every stage only one country or company can perform is a lever waiting to be pulled.

sparks.hook: The industry's famous law was a business commitment, not a physical one.
sparks.insight: The observation that transistor counts double regularly is often described as a law of nature. It was closer to a roadmap the industry agreed to hit: companies coordinated investment, suppliers planned generations of equipment, and customers designed products assuming the improvement would arrive on schedule. Meeting it required extraordinary capital at every step. Treating it as automatic hides how much deliberate and expensive effort each doubling took.
sparks.why: Progress has now slowed on the traditional measure, and gains increasingly come from packaging, specialised architectures and software rather than from shrinking transistors alone.
sparks.apply: Identify one improvement your plan assumes will simply keep arriving, and find out who is actually responsible for delivering it.

sparks.hook: Precision weapons are mostly chips with explosives attached.
sparks.insight: Guided munitions, radar, surveillance and command systems all depend on semiconductors, and the American military advantage from the 1970s onward was built substantially on being ahead in electronics rather than on quantity of equipment. That link explains why chip supply has become a defence question rather than an economic one, and why governments now intervene heavily in an industry they left to the market for forty years.
sparks.why: The defence establishment funded early semiconductor demand when no commercial market existed, so the industry and the military have been entangled from the beginning rather than recently.
sparks.apply: When judging a technology's importance, ask who buys it when there is no commercial market. That customer usually shapes its direction.

sparks.hook: The country that was about to win the chip war in 1988 did not.
sparks.insight: Japanese memory manufacturers took the market with better quality and cheaper capital, and commentary of the period assumed the contest was settled. It was not. Trade pressure, a currency shift, a change in what the industry valued, and Korean competitors arriving with the same strategy reversed it within a decade. Dominance in this industry has repeatedly proved far less durable than it looked at the moment of peak confidence.
sparks.why: This is a useful corrective to current predictions. The record shows leadership changing hands several times, usually when the basis of competition shifted rather than when the leader made an obvious mistake.
sparks.apply: Take the confident industry prediction you hear most often and find the equivalent prediction made thirty years ago, then check how it aged.

sparks.hook: Denying a country machines is easier than denying it knowledge.
sparks.insight: Controls on advanced equipment work because the tools are physical, few in number and produced in allied countries. They are far less effective at stopping the spread of understanding, which travels with people and publications. So restrictions can slow a competitor at the leading edge while doing nothing about the mature technology that most of the economy actually runs on, and while creating a powerful incentive to build a domestic alternative.
sparks.why: This has since been tested directly. Controls tightened in late 2022, and an advanced Chinese-made processor appeared in 2023, which suggests the constraint slowed progress rather than stopping it.
sparks.apply: Before relying on any restriction as a moat, ask what it costs a competitor to route around it and how long that takes them.

sparks.hook: One leading-edge factory costs more than most countries will ever spend.
sparks.insight: Building a plant at the frontier now runs into tens of billions, must be filled with equipment nobody else makes, and has to run near capacity for years to pay back. That economics is why governments announcing domestic chip industries discover the money was the easy part. The scarce inputs are experienced process engineers, supplier ecosystems and the accumulated knowledge of making a specific machine work, none of which can be bought quickly.
sparks.why: The share of usable chips per wafer depends on tacit process knowledge accumulated over years of production. Subsidies buy buildings; they do not buy that knowledge.
sparks.apply: When someone proposes catching up by spending, ask which required inputs cannot be purchased and how long each takes to grow.

sparks.hook: The supply chain that proved globalisation now argues against it.
sparks.insight: Chips are made by a chain crossing a dozen borders, each step performed by whoever does it best, and the result was decades of falling prices and rising performance. Governments are now spending heavily to bring parts of that chain home, accepting higher costs in exchange for lower exposure. Whether that is prudent insurance or expensive duplication depends on a risk nobody can price, and both sides are making the same bet with different confidence.
sparks.why: Reshoring reduces one risk and adds others: smaller scale, higher cost, and subsidised capacity that may not survive once the political attention moves elsewhere.
sparks.apply: Run the numbers on one dependency you would like to bring in-house and state honestly what risk reduction you buy per unit of extra cost.

sparks.hook: The book landed weeks before the export controls it anticipated.
sparks.insight: It was published as the first sweeping restrictions on advanced chip exports to China were announced, and before demand for processors used in machine learning reshaped the industry's economics. Both developments intensified the dynamics it describes rather than contradicting them. The specific numbers, company positions and policy details are now several turns out of date, while the structural argument about chokepoints has only become more visible.
sparks.why: Fast-moving industry books date in their particulars almost immediately. The test worth applying is whether the causal story still explains events the author did not live to see written.
sparks.apply: Read the most recent annual reports of the two companies at the centre of this story before relying on any figure from the book.

actions: Map your product's supply chain down to single-source components, including one tier below your direct suppliers, and mark the exposure.
Write a one-page answer to what your organisation does if its most critical input becomes unavailable for six months.
Check the most confident prediction you hear about this industry against an equivalent prediction made thirty years ago.
Read the latest annual reports of the leading foundry and the leading equipment maker before quoting any figure about the industry.
not_for_you_if: You want the physics of semiconductors or current policy analysis. This is business and diplomatic history, and events since 2022 have moved past its final chapters.

verification.notes: First published 2022, shortly before the October 2022 US export controls. Later developments, including advanced Chinese-made processors in 2023, postdate the book entirely.

title: The Coming Wave
subtitle: Technology, Power, and the Twenty-First Century's Greatest Dilemma
author: Mustafa Suleyman with Michael Bhaskar
why_it_matters: It put containment at the centre of the AI debate, argued from inside the labs building these systems, and treated engineered biology and machine intelligence as one wave rather than two. It shaped much of the vocabulary policymakers now use.

crux.headline: Powerful technology gets cheaper, and cheap things spread
crux.body: Every general technology follows the same path: it works, it gets cheaper, it gets copied, and eventually anyone can have it. Machine intelligence and engineered biology are on that path now, and both hand small groups capabilities that used to require a state. Containing them is probably impossible and abandoning them is also unacceptable, which leaves a narrow and uncomfortable route between the two.

sparks.hook: You cannot uninvent a technology, and you cannot stop it getting cheap.
sparks.insight: Anything that works spreads. Costs fall, knowledge diffuses, copies appear, and what once required a national programme becomes a purchase. This happened with engines, electricity, computers and weapons, and there is no example of a genuinely useful technology being permanently held back by whoever had it first. Planning on the assumption that you will keep your advantage is planning for the one outcome history reliably does not supply.
sparks.why: Diffusion is driven by demand and by the falling cost of replication, not by the intentions of the originator. Restrictions have delayed the spread of things; they have not prevented it.
sparks.apply: For any capability you are protecting, write down how long you actually expect the lead to last and plan for the world after it ends.

sparks.hook: The barrier to causing serious harm keeps falling, and falling fast.
sparks.insight: Capabilities that once required a laboratory, a budget and a team now require a laptop and access. That is straightforwardly good for medicine, engineering and research, and it means the number of people able to cause large-scale damage rises along the same curve. The uncomfortable part is that these are not separable. The tools that let a small lab design a treatment are the tools that lower the barrier everywhere else.
sparks.why: The dual-use problem is old, but the scale is new because the marginal cost of copying software and biological designs is close to zero once the first version exists.
sparks.apply: Add one question to your risk register: what does your product enable for a capable, hostile user operating with no budget at all?

sparks.hook: Every proposed way of controlling this wave has a hole in it.
sparks.insight: Slowing research pushes it elsewhere. Banning it drives it underground. Licensing it favours large incumbents. Publishing openly spreads capability to everyone, including the people you least want to have it. Relying on companies to govern themselves relies on companies. None is sufficient alone, and the argument here is for many overlapping partial measures rather than one solution, on the theory that layers of imperfect friction buy time even where no layer is watertight.
sparks.why: The case for layered mitigation is borrowed from safety engineering, where no single barrier is ever trusted. Critics reasonably note that this framing can justify almost any measure while committing to none.
sparks.apply: For one risk your organisation faces, list four independent partial mitigations instead of searching for a single complete fix.

carousel.title: Technical safeguards
carousel.body: Build limits into the systems: evaluation before release, refusal behaviour, monitoring in production. Necessary, and routinely defeated by determined users.

carousel.title: Audits and accountability
carousel.body: Independent inspection of what a system can actually do, with consequences attached. Works only where inspectors have real access and real power.

carousel.title: Choke points
carousel.body: Control the scarce inputs: advanced chips, specialised equipment, key materials. The most effective lever available and also the most temporary one.

carousel.title: Public capability
carousel.body: Governments that understand the technology can regulate it. Regulators who depend entirely on the industry for expertise cannot.

carousel.title: Culture inside the labs
carousel.body: Norms among the people building these systems matter most in the years before rules exist, and least once serious commercial pressure arrives.

sparks.hook: The state's monopoly on serious capability is quietly ending.
sparks.insight: Governments have historically held the things that could do large-scale damage or provide large-scale services: weapons, surveillance, infrastructure. Widely available intelligence and biological tools erode that from both directions. Private actors gain capabilities states used to monopolise, and states gain tools of control they never had before. The result is not simply weaker or stronger government but a redistribution that existing institutions were not built to handle.
sparks.why: The argument is plausible and hard to test. Comparable predictions about earlier technologies dissolving the nation state have consistently turned out to be premature.
sparks.apply: Ask which functions your government performs today that a private system could perform next year, and who is accountable if it does.

sparks.hook: Refusing to consider the bad case is a bias, not a temperament.
sparks.insight: People in and around technology systematically discount warnings, partly because most predicted catastrophes have not happened and partly because pessimism is socially and commercially costly. That produces a discourse where raising a serious risk marks you as unserious. The correction is not to become gloomy but to insist that a low-probability, high-consequence outcome deserves engineering attention rather than a change of subject.
sparks.why: The framing is useful and also self-serving, since it lets the author's own warnings count as clear sight and criticism of them count as bias. Apply it in both directions or not at all.
sparks.apply: In your next planning session, assign one person the explicit job of arguing the failure case and write their objections into the record.

carousel.title: Assign the role explicitly
carousel.body: Someone is asked to argue the failure case, on the record, as their job. Volunteering to be the pessimist is a career cost nobody should pay.

carousel.title: Describe the failure concretely
carousel.body: Not that risk exists, but that this specific thing goes wrong in this specific way. Vague warnings are easy to nod at and impossible to act on.

carousel.title: Weigh consequence, not just odds
carousel.body: Low probability with unrecoverable consequences deserves engineering, not a percentage. Ask what cannot be undone, separately from what is likely.

carousel.title: Write it into the decision
carousel.body: Objections that vanish from the record teach everyone that raising them is pointless. Keep them attached to the decision they were made about.

sparks.hook: Everyone building this agrees it should be slower. Nobody slows down.
sparks.insight: Competition between companies and between countries makes unilateral caution expensive. If you pause and your competitor does not, you lose position and they set the standard, so restraint requires coordination that nobody can enforce. This is why voluntary commitments tend to be strongest in exactly the areas that cost least, and why the people warning most loudly about the risks are frequently the same people accelerating toward them.
sparks.why: This is a familiar collective action problem, and the author's own position running major AI efforts is both the source of the insight and its clearest available illustration.
sparks.apply: Before trusting any voluntary commitment, ask what it costs the party making it. Commitments that cost nothing predict nothing.

sparks.hook: Machine learning and engineered biology are the same story told twice.
sparks.insight: Both are general-purpose, both are getting rapidly cheaper, both let a small group produce effects that used to need an institution, and both increasingly feed each other as models are used to design biological systems. Treating them as separate policy areas, handled by different agencies with different expertise, misses the fact that the capabilities converge. This convergence argument is the most original part of the book and the least covered elsewhere.
sparks.why: The technical link is real and growing, though the timelines for biological design tools remain considerably more uncertain than the confident tone here suggests.
sparks.apply: If you work in AI policy, spend an afternoon reading about biosecurity governance. The failure modes and the debates rhyme closely.

sparks.hook: The containment argument was overtaken by events almost immediately.
sparks.insight: Since publication, capable models with published weights have spread widely, which is close to the scenario the book treats as its hard case. Meanwhile the concentration of frontier capability in a few large firms, and the enormous capital those systems require, has proved a stronger constraint than any regulation. The prediction that proliferation would be the central difficulty holds. The assumption that policy could meaningfully shape the pace looks weaker than it did.
sparks.why: Books about the next decade written by participants are useful for framing and unreliable on timing. This one's structural claims have held up considerably better than its policy expectations.
sparks.apply: When reading forecasts, separate the mechanism from the schedule. Mechanisms transfer between eras; dates almost never do.

sparks.hook: Read this knowing who wrote it and what they were selling.
sparks.insight: The argument comes from a co-founder of a leading AI lab who has since run one of the largest corporate AI efforts in the world. That gives genuine inside knowledge of how these systems get built and a clear interest in the outcome, including in regulation that established players can absorb more easily than newcomers. Neither fact makes the argument wrong. Both are relevant to how much weight you give its specific recommendations.
sparks.why: Calls for regulation from incumbents have a well-documented tendency to produce rules that entrench incumbents. That pattern is worth checking against every specific proposal here.
sparks.apply: For any policy proposal you read, spend two minutes working out who it advantages, and do that before deciding whether you agree with it.

sparks.hook: The choice is not between stopping this and letting it run.
sparks.insight: One side says halt, which forfeits enormous benefits and does not work anyway. The other says build and adapt, which quietly assumes the damage will be recoverable. The position argued here is a narrow route between them: keep developing while building real capacity to inspect, refuse and correct, and accept that this requires institutions we currently do not have. It is less satisfying than either extreme, which is a point in its favour.
sparks.why: Nothing here establishes that the narrow path is achievable, and the mechanisms proposed remain largely aspirational. It is a framing of the problem rather than a solution to it.
sparks.apply: In your next argument about a risky technology, state the strongest version of both extremes before offering any middle position.

actions: Add one line to your risk register: what your product enables for a capable, hostile user operating with no budget.
Assign a named person to argue the failure case in your next major decision, and record their objections in the decision document.
For one risk you face, design four independent partial mitigations instead of searching for a single complete answer.
For every AI policy proposal you read this month, work out which existing players it advantages before deciding what you think.
not_for_you_if: You want technical detail or a neutral analyst. It is a broad, urgent argument written by an industry participant with a direct stake in its conclusions.

verification.notes: First published 2023, co-written with Michael Bhaskar. Suleyman co-founded DeepMind and Inflection AI and later led Microsoft's AI division; several policy expectations here have been overtaken by the spread of open-weight models.

title: Technopoly
subtitle: The Surrender of Culture to Technology
author: Neil Postman
why_it_matters: It argued that technology is never neutral and that every tool carries a philosophy inside it. Written before the web existed, it anticipated the shape of the argument we are still having about attention, data and expertise.

crux.headline: Every tool arrives with an argument built into it
crux.body: A technology is not a neutral instrument that leaves the world otherwise unchanged. It redistributes attention, status and power, makes some questions easy to ask and others invisible, and creates winners and losers who are rarely the same people. The right question about any new tool is not whether it works but what it displaces, who gains from it, and whose problem it was actually built to solve.

sparks.hook: Ask what a new technology takes away, not just what it adds.
sparks.insight: New tools are sold as additions: the same life, plus a capability. They are never that. A tool changes what is easy, and what is easy becomes what is done, so other practices quietly stop. The clock made time measurable and turned the day into something to be divided and sold. Printing made argument portable and made memory less necessary. The addition gets advertised and the subtraction is discovered later by people who never voted for it.
sparks.why: This is a claim about second-order effects, which are genuinely hard to evidence in advance. The historical examples convince; the predictive power is weaker than the confident tone implies.
sparks.apply: For the next tool your team adopts, write down which practice it will replace, then check in three months whether you miss that practice.

sparks.hook: Every technology has winners and losers, and they are different people.
sparks.insight: Ask who benefits from a change and the answer is rarely everybody. Printing empowered authors and publishers and weakened the scribes and the institutions that controlled interpretation. Television advantaged people who are compelling on camera. Ranking systems advantage whoever produces material that holds attention. The distribution question gets skipped because benefits are described in general terms while the costs land on specific, identifiable groups.
sparks.why: The framing holds up well, though it can slide into treating any redistribution as a loss for society rather than as a change in who currently holds the advantage.
sparks.apply: For a technology your organisation is adopting, name the group whose work becomes less valuable and decide what you owe them.

sparks.hook: When information became abundant, the scarce thing became a reason to care.
sparks.insight: For most of history the problem was getting information, and the institutions we inherited, including schools, editors and professions, were built to solve scarcity. Once information became effectively unlimited those defences stopped working, and abundance without a framework for deciding what matters produces noise rather than understanding. The prediction was made about television and photocopiers, which makes it more impressive rather than less that it describes a feed.
sparks.why: The diagnosis has aged extremely well. The remedy proposed, a return to coherent cultural narratives that give information meaning, is vague and has not happened anywhere.
sparks.apply: Cut one information source from your week entirely and notice whether any decision you made would have gone differently without it.

sparks.hook: Once a number exists, it starts making decisions on your behalf.
sparks.insight: Turning a complicated human question into a score makes it manageable, and makes the parts that resisted counting disappear from the conversation. A test score becomes intelligence, a grade becomes learning, an engagement rate becomes value. This is not an argument against measurement, which is among the most powerful things people ever invented. It is an argument that a number always leaves something out, and the thing it leaves out stops being discussed at all.
sparks.why: The critique of standardised testing here draws on real and continuing debates about what such tests measure. It is also true that resistance to measurement often protects unaccountable judgement.
sparks.apply: Take one metric that drives decisions in your team and write down everything it cannot see, then bring that list to the next review.

sparks.hook: The strongest ideologies are the ones that look like plumbing.
sparks.insight: A technology becomes truly powerful when it stops looking like a choice. Nobody argues about whether to use a clock or an alphabet. They are simply how things are, and the assumptions they carry go permanently unexamined. That is what makes infrastructure political in a way that is hard to discuss: by the time a tool has become invisible, its embedded assumptions have become common sense, and questioning them sounds eccentric rather than reasonable.
sparks.why: This explains why the most consequential technology debates happen at the moment of adoption. Once a tool is ordinary, reopening the argument is nearly impossible.
sparks.apply: Name one system at work nobody questions because it is simply how things are done, and ask out loud what it optimises for.

sparks.hook: Ask which problem a new technology solves and who had that problem.
sparks.insight: Innovations arrive as answers, and the question they answer is often nobody's. A great deal of technology solves problems for the organisation deploying it, around cost, control and measurement, while being described as a benefit to the person using it. Self-service checkouts move labour onto customers. Productivity monitoring solves a management problem. Asking whose problem is being solved is the fastest way to see through the framing.
sparks.why: This test is reliable and easy to apply. It does not settle whether the change is good or bad, only who is actually being served by it.
sparks.apply: For the next system introduced at your work, write one sentence naming whose problem it solves, and say that sentence out loud in the meeting.

sparks.hook: People who understand a technology decide things nobody asked them about.
sparks.insight: As systems grow complex, authority drifts toward whoever can operate them. Decisions that are really about values, such as what a school should teach, how a hospital should triage, or what a feed should show, get resolved as technical questions by whoever is able to implement them. That transfer happens quietly, without anyone deciding it should, and it is very hard to reverse because reversing it means non-experts arguing on the experts' ground.
sparks.why: This is visible today whenever a product decision with obvious ethical content is settled in practice by whoever writes the ranking function.
sparks.apply: Find one decision on your team framed as technical that is really about values, and name it as such in writing.

sparks.hook: The only defence offered here is teaching people to ask better questions.
sparks.insight: The proposed remedy is not regulation or refusal but education: teaching history so people can see that arrangements were chosen, teaching how language shapes what can be thought, teaching where ideas came from. It is a thin answer to an enormous problem and Postman knew it. It is also the only one that does not require an authority to decide on everyone's behalf, which is why it is worth taking seriously despite being obviously insufficient.
sparks.why: Education as a defence against manipulation has a mixed record. Media literacy programmes have produced modest and inconsistent effects when evaluated properly.
sparks.apply: Teach one person on your team the history of a tool you both use, including what it replaced and who objected to it at the time.

carousel.title: Learn what it replaced
carousel.body: Every tool displaced something. Knowing what, and who defended the older thing, converts an apparent inevitability into a decision people actually made.

carousel.title: Learn who objected
carousel.body: The critics at the time were usually wrong about some things and right about others. Sorting which is which is the actual skill worth having.

carousel.title: Notice the vocabulary
carousel.body: Tools bring words that quietly settle arguments: users, engagement, content, resources. Ask what each one hides about the thing it names.

carousel.title: Practise the counterfactual
carousel.body: Ask how this could have been built differently. If no alternative is imaginable, you have accepted a design as though it were a law of nature.

sparks.hook: He was writing about television and described the internet by accident.
sparks.insight: The book predates the web, social platforms and machine learning entirely, and its examples now feel quaint. But the structure of the argument, abundance without judgement, measurement crowding out meaning, authority migrating to whoever runs the machine, maps onto the present so closely that it reads as prophecy. What has not aged well is the nostalgia, the sense that some earlier arrangement was coherent in a way ours is not.
sparks.why: Critics have long argued that Postman romanticises a past that was neither as thoughtful nor as inclusive as he implies, and that his pessimism admits no test that could disprove it.
sparks.apply: Notice when a critique of technology depends on a golden age, then ask when that age was and who it was actually good for.

sparks.hook: You do not have to choose between enthusiasm and refusal.
sparks.insight: The useful stance is neither the boosterism that treats every new capability as progress nor the rejection that treats every tool as decline. It is the habit of asking, before adoption, what this changes, who it serves, what it makes harder, and what would count as evidence that it went wrong. That takes about ten minutes and is almost never done, because the alternative, deciding by whether something feels modern, takes none.
sparks.why: The middle position is analytically demanding and rhetorically weak, which is why public technology debate collapses into two camps who each treat the other as the entire problem.
sparks.apply: Write four questions on a card for your next adoption decision: what changes, who gains, what gets harder, and what would prove this wrong.

carousel.title: What changes in practice
carousel.body: Not the feature list. Which specific daily activity happens differently afterwards, and who is doing it now that was not doing it before.

carousel.title: Who gains and who pays
carousel.body: Name the group whose work becomes more valuable and the group whose becomes less. If they look like the same people, look harder.

carousel.title: What becomes harder
carousel.body: Every tool makes something easy and something else awkward. The awkward thing quietly stops happening, so name it while you still can.

carousel.title: What would prove this wrong
carousel.body: Decide in advance what evidence would mean the adoption failed, and set a date to look. Otherwise it succeeds by default, permanently.

actions: Before your team's next tool adoption, write one page naming what it changes, who gains, what becomes harder, and what would count as evidence it failed.
Take one metric that drives decisions where you work and list everything it cannot see, then bring that list to the next review.
Cut one information source from your week entirely and check whether any decision would have gone differently without it.
Identify one decision framed as technical on your team that is actually about values, and say so in writing.
not_for_you_if: You want practical guidance or an even-handed assessment. It is a polemic, written before the web, and far more convincing about diagnosis than about cure.

verification.notes: First published 1992, seven years after Amusing Ourselves to Death. Postman died in 2003, so nothing here addresses social platforms or machine learning directly.

title: Refactoring
subtitle: Improving the Design of Existing Code
author: Martin Fowler
why_it_matters: It turned tidying code from an unbilled indulgence into a named, disciplined practice with a catalogue of safe moves. The word itself, and the fact that every serious editor now has a menu for it, comes from this line of work.

crux.headline: Change the structure without changing the behaviour
crux.body: Refactoring is a specific discipline, not a synonym for rewriting. You make small changes that leave what the program does exactly the same while making it easier to understand and change, and you verify after each step that nothing broke. Done that way, improving a design stops being a risky project you must request permission for and becomes something you do continuously while adding features.

sparks.hook: Refactoring is not rewriting, and confusing them has cost fortunes.
sparks.insight: The discipline has a strict definition: change the internal structure while the external behaviour stays identical, in steps small enough that you can check after each one. Rewriting is different, with new behaviour, new bugs, months of parallel systems and a launch date that slips. Most projects that describe themselves as refactoring are actually rewriting, which is why the word has such a bad reputation among managers who have been burned by one.
sparks.why: The distinction is what makes the practice safe. Once behaviour changes in the same step as structure, you can no longer tell which of the two caused a failure.
sparks.apply: Before your next cleanup, write down what behaviour must stay identical. If you cannot, you are planning a rewrite and should say so out loud.

sparks.hook: Without tests you are not refactoring, you are just hoping.
sparks.insight: The whole method depends on being able to tell, quickly and reliably, that behaviour did not change. That is what a test suite is for here: not proving correctness in general, but detecting whether a structural change broke something. On code with no tests, the first move is building enough of a safety net around the part you are touching, which is often more work than the cleanup itself and is not optional.
sparks.why: The step size you can safely take is set by how fast and how trustworthy your feedback is. Slow or flaky tests force larger, riskier changes with no way to localise a failure.
sparks.apply: Pick the messiest function you own, write tests that pin its current behaviour including the odd parts, and only then change anything.

carousel.title: Pin the current behaviour
carousel.body: Write tests describing what the code does now, including the wrong bits. You are recording behaviour at this stage, not endorsing it.

carousel.title: Make the tests fast
carousel.body: A suite taking ten minutes gets run once an hour. The value of the safety net comes entirely from running it after every small step.

carousel.title: Change exactly one thing
carousel.body: One structural move, then run the tests. When something breaks you want a suspect list containing exactly one entry.

carousel.title: Commit at every green
carousel.body: Small committed steps mean you can always return to something that worked. A long uncommitted refactor is a rewrite wearing a disguise.

sparks.hook: You cannot always say why code is bad, but you can learn to smell it.
sparks.insight: Judgement about design is hard to teach, so the useful move is naming the recurring signs: a function grown too long to hold in your head, the same logic copied in four places, a class that knows too much about another one, a parameter list that keeps growing. None of these is automatically wrong. Each is a prompt to look, and having names for them turns vague unease into something a team can discuss without it becoming personal.
sparks.why: Naming the symptom rather than judging the author is what makes code review survivable. The signs are heuristics rather than rules, and applying them mechanically creates its own mess.
sparks.apply: In your next code review, describe one problem by naming the pattern rather than the person, and propose the specific structural move that fixes it.

sparks.hook: Safety comes from the size of the step, not the skill of the developer.
sparks.insight: Experienced developers do not make bigger leaps. They make smaller ones and take them faster. Each move is small enough that if the tests fail the cause is obvious, and small enough to abandon cheaply. This feels absurdly slow the first time and turns out to be faster overall, because the time normally lost is not in making changes but in working out which of forty simultaneous changes broke the build.
sparks.why: Debugging cost rises sharply with the number of changes made since the last known good state. Shrinking that number is the entire mechanism behind the discipline.
sparks.apply: Take a change you would normally do in one commit, split it into five with the tests run between each, and time both approaches honestly.

carousel.title: Find the last good state
carousel.body: Everything rests on being able to return to something that worked. Commit before you start, with the tests passing and nothing in progress.

carousel.title: Make one structural move
carousel.body: A single rename, extraction or relocation. Resist doing the obvious next thing in the same step, however tempting it is at the time.

carousel.title: Run the tests immediately
carousel.body: Every step ends with a check. If the check is slow, that is a problem to fix before continuing rather than one to work around.

carousel.title: Commit on green, then repeat
carousel.body: A chain of small verified commits can be bisected, reviewed and reverted individually. One enormous commit can do none of those things.

sparks.hook: Sometimes the right answer is to leave the mess exactly where it is.
sparks.insight: Not all bad code deserves attention. Code nobody reads, nobody changes, and that works is not costing you anything, and improving it spends real time for no return at all. Refactoring pays when you are about to work in an area and its current shape makes that work harder. It also has a genuine failure case: code so tangled that rewriting from the specification is cheaper, assuming you can still recover what the specification was.
sparks.why: The cost of poor structure is only paid when somebody has to change it. Stable code nobody touches has effectively no design debt, however ugly it looks from outside.
sparks.apply: Before cleaning anything, check the file's change history. If nothing has been modified in two years, leave it alone and move on.

sparks.hook: Reshape the code until your new feature becomes obvious to add.
sparks.insight: When a feature is awkward to add, the instinct is to force it in with a flag or a special case. The alternative is to first restructure the existing code so the new feature slots in naturally, without adding the feature during that step. The restructuring is verifiable because behaviour has not changed, and the feature afterwards is small enough to review properly. Two clean steps beat one tangled one every time.
sparks.why: Separating structural work from behavioural work means each commit carries only one kind of risk, which makes review, testing and rollback all dramatically simpler.
sparks.apply: Next time a feature feels awkward, stop and ask what shape would make it trivial, then do that reshaping as its own separate commit.

sparks.hook: Plenty of good engineers think continuous refactoring is a bad habit.
sparks.insight: The counter-argument runs like this: constant restructuring churns the code, invalidates everyone else's mental model, creates enormous review load, and often chases an aesthetic ideal rather than a business need. Teams have shipped excellent software while leaving ugly code alone for years. The honest position is that this is a tool with a real cost, most valuable in code under active change and least valuable once it becomes an identity.
sparks.why: The dispute is real and unresolved. Empirical evidence that refactoring improves long-run maintainability is considerably thinner than the strength of opinion on either side would suggest.
sparks.apply: Justify your next refactor in one sentence about work you are about to do. If the sentence is about beauty, put it back on the shelf.

sparks.hook: The cheapest improvement available to you is a better name.
sparks.insight: Most of the difficulty in reading code is working out what things are. A variable called data, a function named after how it works rather than what it delivers, a class named after a pattern instead of a responsibility: each forces the reader to reconstruct intent from scratch. Renaming is the lowest-risk change available with modern tools and it improves every future reading. It is also the change people are most embarrassed to submit, which is why so much stays badly named.
sparks.why: Code is read far more often than it is written, so anything reducing reading cost compounds. Naming is the highest-leverage version of that with almost no risk attached.
sparks.apply: Rename three things this week whose names made you pause when you read them, and do it as a separate commit with no other change in it.

sparks.hook: The same logic in four places will be fixed in three of them.
sparks.insight: Copied code is not wrong in itself, but it guarantees that some future change gets applied inconsistently, because whoever makes it will find some copies and miss others. The standard response is to pull the shared behaviour into one place. The standard failure is doing that too early: two things that look alike today but change for different reasons will fight inside a shared abstraction, and untangling that is harder than the duplication ever was.
sparks.why: The cost of a wrong abstraction usually exceeds the cost of duplication, which is why many experienced developers now wait for a third occurrence before unifying anything.
sparks.apply: Find one duplicated block and check whether the copies change for the same reason. Unify them only if the answer is yes.

sparks.hook: Your editor performs these moves safely. Most people still do them by hand.
sparks.insight: Automated tools can perform many of these structural changes without altering behaviour, which removes most of the risk and nearly all of the tedium. The catalogue of moves was compiled when almost none of this was automated, and the second edition, written twenty years later in a different language, reflects a world where tools handle the mechanical part and judgement about when to act is what remains.
sparks.why: Tool support is uneven across languages, and dynamically typed languages resist safe automated transformation, so the manual discipline still matters wherever the tooling is weak.
sparks.apply: Learn the three refactoring shortcuts in your editor this week and use them instead of editing by hand for one full working day.

actions: Pick the function you dread most, write tests that pin its current behaviour, and only then improve its structure in small committed steps.
Split your next change into a structural commit that alters no behaviour and a behavioural commit that alters no structure.
Check the change history of any file before cleaning it up, and leave alone anything nobody has touched in two years.
Learn the refactoring shortcuts in your editor and spend one full day using them instead of hand-editing code.
not_for_you_if: You do not write code, or you want architecture rather than local craft. Much of it is a catalogue you consult rather than a book you read straight through.

verification.notes: First published 1999 with Kent Beck contributing; a second edition in 2018 rewrote the examples in JavaScript. Whether continuous refactoring pays off is genuinely disputed among practitioners.
